1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	Three limits of `ledger.py` (below):
55	
56	- A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no further note.
57	- No command edits a row's claim. `close --claim` takes a corrected one.
58	- Its heading reader does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
59	
60	## Reading the record
61	
62	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
63	
64	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
65	
66	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
67	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
68	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
69	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
70	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
71	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
72	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
73	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
74	
75	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
76	
77	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
78	
79	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
80	
81	## Writing to the record
82	
83	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
84	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
85	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
86	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
87	  - what it means for the work;
88	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
89	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
90	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
91	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
92	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
93	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
94	
95	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
96	
97	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
98	
99	To add a row:
100	
101	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
102	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
103	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
104	
105	To change a row:
106	
107	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N.
108	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
109	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
117	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
118	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
119

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28	
29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
30	
31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
32	
33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
34	
35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
36	
37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
38	
39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
40	
41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
42	
43	## Building it
44	
45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
46	
47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
48	
49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
52	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
53	
54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
55	
56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
59	
60	## Citing it
61	
62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

84	== Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:313-540
85	
86	\section{Where Clauses}
87	\seclabel{where-clauses}
88	
89	\note{The \KWD{where} clause syntax in this section is out of date.}
90	
91	\begin{Grammar}
92	\emph{Where} &::=& \KWD{where} \{ \emph{WhereClauseList} \}\\
93	\emph{WhereClauseList} &::=& \emph{WhereClause}(\EXP{,}
94	\emph{WhereClause})$^*$ \\
95	\emph{WhereClause} &::=& \emph{Id} \emph{Extends}\\
96	&$|$& \emph{TypeAlias} \\
97	&$|$& \emph{NatConstraint} \\
98	&$|$& \emph{IntConstraint} \\
99	&$|$& \emph{BoolConstraint} \\
100	&$|$& \emph{UnitConstraint} \\
101	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{coerces} \emph{TypeRef}\\
102	&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{widens} \emph{TypeRef}\\
103	\end{Grammar}
104	
105	
106	Static parameters may have constraints placed on them
107	in a \KWD{where} clause.
108	A \KWD{where} clause begins with
109	\KWD{where}, followed by a sequence of static
110	parameter constraints enclosed in braces \EXP{\{} and \EXP{\}},
111	and separated by commas.
112	
113	
114	A \KWD{where} clause may introduce new static variables, i.e., identifiers
115	for types and other static entities that may not be static parameters.
116	We use the term \emph{\KWD{where}-clause variables} to refer to
117	static variables that are not also static parameters.
118	The \KWD{where}-clause variables must be bound in a \KWD{where} clause.
119	
120	
121	A static parameter constraint is one of the following forms:
122	\begin{itemize}
123	\item a trait constraint consisting of the identifier of
124	a naked type variable, followed by \KWD{extends}
125	followed by a set of trait references which may include naked type variables,
126	\item a type alias (described in \secref{type-alias}),
127	\item an arithmetic constraint,
128	\item a boolean constraint,
129	\item a unit equality constraint,
130	\item a \KWD{coerces} constraint (described in
131	  \secref{coercion-declarations}), or
132	\item a \KWD{widens} constraint (described in
133	  \secref{coercion-declarations}).
134	\end{itemize}
135	A \KWD{where} clause may include mutually recursive constraints.
136	All static variables in a trait, object, or functional declaration must
137	occur either as a static parameter or as a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
138	\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
139	\KWD{where} clauses.
140	
141	An entry of an \KWD{extends} clause may carry a \KWD{where} clause of its
142	own (\secref{trait-decls}).
143	If that clause introduces no \KWD{where}-clause variable and all its
144	constraints are trait constraints, the declared trait or object extends the
145	entry's type exactly where the constraints hold:
146	an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type,
147	and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not.
148	Within the declaration the constraints hold: the entry itself and the
149	declaration's members are checked as if the constraints were in the
150	declaration's own \KWD{where} clause, and the other entries of its
151	\KWD{extends} clause are checked without them.
152	So a list is totally ordered exactly where its elements are:
153	%trait List[\E\] extends { ZeroIndexed[\E\],
154	%    LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] } }
155	%end
156	\begin{Fortress}
157	\(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket \KWD{extends} \{\TYP{ZeroIndexed}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,\)\\
158	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \TYP{LexicographicOrder}\llbracket\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,E\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{E \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket\}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
159	\(\KWD{end}\)
160	\end{Fortress}
161	\revision{revival-conditional}{This paragraph and its example are new.
162	The Working Draft of February 2011 gave each entry of an \KWD{extends}
163	clause an optional \KWD{where} clause in its grammar and stated no meaning
164	for it, and its front matter lists conditional extension among the
165	features not yet supported.}
166	
167	A \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static argument
168	in an \KWD{extends} clause.
169	Such an occurrence would make the declared trait or object a subtype of
170	one instantiation for each type that the variable may stand for,
171	which instantiation exclusion forbids
172	(\secref{trait-types} and \secref{trait-decls});
173	the second of the three declarations below shows why.
174	\revision{revival-where}{This restriction is new.
175	The three declarations that follow were offered as legal by the
176	Working Draft of February 2011; they are kept as examples of what is not
177	allowed, each with the way to write it.}
178	
179	In particular, a trait declaration may not extend other instantiations
180	of itself through a \KWD{where}-clause variable.
181	The following declaration would express that the static parameter \VAR{S}
182	of \VAR{C} is covariant, making \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} a subtype of
183	\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S};
184	it is not allowed:
185	%(* Not allowed! *)
186	%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
187	%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
188	%end
189	\begin{Fortress}
190	\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
191	\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
192	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
193	\(\KWD{end}\)
194	\end{Fortress}
195	Static parameters are invariant:
196	\EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
197	only if \VAR{S} and \VAR{T} are the same type.
198	A value of one instantiation is widened to another by a function
199	whose bounded static parameters state that one argument extends the other:
200	%trait C[\S\]
201	%  getter item(): S
202	%end
203	%object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
204	%widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
205	\begin{Fortress}
206	\(\KWD{trait}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket\)\\
207	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter}\:\VAR{item}()\COLON S\)\-\\\poptabs
208	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
209	\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}S\rrbracket(\VAR{item}\COLON S) \KWD{extends}\:C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)\\
210	\(\VAR{widen}\llbracket{}T, S \KWD{extends}\:T\rrbracket(c\COLON C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket)\COLON C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket = \TYP{CItem}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(c.\VAR{item})\)
211	\end{Fortress}
212	so that, where a trait \TYP{Dog} extends a trait \TYP{Animal} and \VAR{d}
213	is a \EXP{C\llbracket\TYP{Dog}\rrbracket},
214	\EXP{\VAR{widen}\llbracket\TYP{Animal}, \TYP{Dog}\rrbracket(d)} is a

228	Trait declarations need not have any static parameters in order
229	to have a \KWD{where} clause. But the following trait
230	declaration is not allowed:
231	%(* Not allowed! *)
232	%trait C extends D[\T\]
233	%  where {T extends Object}
234	%end
235	\begin{Fortress}
236	\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
237	\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{extends} D\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
238	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
239	\(\KWD{end}\)
240	\end{Fortress}
241	In this declaration, trait \VAR{C} would be a subtrait of \emph{every}
242	instantiation of parametric trait \VAR{D}. Thus, trait \VAR{C} would have all
243	of the methods of every instantiation of \VAR{D}. By thinking of the
244	declaration this way, we can see what restrictions we need to impose on
245	the trait \VAR{C} in order for it to be sensible. If trait
246	\VAR{C} inherits a method declaration that refers to \VAR{T}, it really
247	contains infinitely many methods (one for each instantiation of \VAR{T}).

249	explicit from the program text as static parameters are.
250	It must be possible to infer which method is referred to at the call site.
251	%%So every method invocation is annotated with static types by type inference.
252	If there is not enough information to infer which method is called,
253	type checking rejects the

258	different instantiations of \VAR{D},

261	that is why it is not allowed.

3	# Climb batch 18: the judge's ruling on the merged-diff review
4	
5	Written 2026-10-18 by the batch's judge, on `main` at `7d6c65881`. Nothing was built or run for this ruling, and the gate's folders were not read. Each point below is a reading of the tree at that commit, marked "by reading" where no run backs it, or a result that the review quotes with its command.
6	
7	## 1. Ruling
8	
9	**Decision: repair.** The review's one blocking finding is upheld, and its repair is taken with one addition.
10	
11	- The finding concerns rung X. `TypeWellFormedChecker`'s trait and object declaration cases check five parts of the declaration with every conditional `extends` entry's conditions holding: the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, its `throws` clause and contract (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:194-195`, `:211-212`), and its `excludes` and `comprises` clauses (`:202`). The base checks them with the declaration's own `where` clause only. These parts hold at every instance of the declared type, so they are checked without the conditions.
12	- The addition: `Decls` type-checks an object's contract with the same conditions holding (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:134-142`). It is the same defect in the other checker that X edited, and the specification sentence the repair writes would be false of it.
13	- The value parameters, the members and `self` keep the conditions (P-151). The line between the two kinds of part is section 3's. Where it falls for the value parameters is listed for the curator (section 6).
14	
15	The decision cannot be land: the repair edits two Scala files of the checker and the specification. The edit is under `ProjectFortress/src/`, a path the gate reads, so the gate runs again after the repair (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:1273`, `:1352-1353`).
16	
17	## 2. What the tree does
18	
19	The trait case (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:187-203`) and the object case (`:204-220`):
20	
21	- `:194` and `:211` set the analyzer to `analyzer.extend(sparams, KindEnv.withExtendsConditions(where, extendsC))`, whose `where` clause holds the conditions of every conditional entry (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/staticenv/KindEnv.scala:179-203`).
22	- With that analyzer, `:195` and `:212` walk `sparams`, `where`, `throwsC` and `contract`, and `:202` walks `params`, `decls`, `self`, `excludes` and `comprises`.
23	- Only the `extends` entries are walked another way (`:197-201`, `:214-218`, the skeptic's upheld `bd18b6a47`). Where another entry is conditional, each entry is walked with the declaration's `where` clause and its own conditions.
24	- Rung K's check of a type's own `where` constraints at its use (`:259-289`) reads the same `analyzer` (`:281`). So it is lifted with the static-argument bounds (`:248-258`) wherever the header is walked.
25	
26	The review ran three programs with `bin/fortress typecheck` on the merged tree (`/home/user/fortress-gather18`) and on the base build through `old-fortress.sh` (its blockingCode entry, quoted here):
27	
28	- (1) `trait Shows end` `trait W[\T extends Shows\] end` `trait D[\E\] extends { Shows where { E extends Shows } } excludes { W[\E\] } end`: main exit=0; base 'ExclBound.fss:6:69-72: Ill-formed type: W[\E\] The static argument E does not satisfy the corresponding bound Shows.' exit=255.
29	- (2) the same `D` with `comprises { V[\E\] }` and `object V[\T extends Shows\]() extends D[\T\] end`: main exit=0; base 'CompBound.fss:5:70-73: Ill-formed type: V[\E\]' exit=255.
30	- (3) `trait D[\E, F extends W[\E\]\] extends { Shows where { E extends Shows } } end`: main exit=0; base 'ParamBound.fss:6:23-26: Ill-formed type: W[\E\]' exit=255.
31	- K's face: an `excludes` entry `W[\E\]` for `trait W[\T\] where { T extends Shows }` is accepted beside the conditional entry (main exit=0) and refused without it (main 'ExclPlain.fss:6:25-28: Ill-formed type: W[\E\]').
32	
33	The same holds of the object's contract in `Decls`, by reading. `checkerWSparams` holds every condition (`Decls.scala:135-136`). The contract is checked with `method_checker` (`:139-142`), which at that point is `checkerWSparams` (`:137`). The base checked it with `this.extend(sparams, params, where)`, as `git show db8fecd22:ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala` shows at the same place. No run backs this; the repair's first test run measures it (section 5, step 3).
34	
35	## 3. What the text and the record say
36	
37	**The decision.** P-151 (POSITIONS.md, **Only the `where` forms the team wrote down are built.**) puts two things under a conditional entry's condition. The trait "is that type only where the condition holds, and its members are checked under the condition". The curator's accepted reading names the same two: "the condition holds inside the declaration while its members and overrides are checked, as Swift, Rust and Haskell check it" (`explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md:30`). Neither names the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, its contract, or its `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. In each of those three languages, a conformance's condition holds only in that conformance's own items. The type's parameters and their bounds are checked without it, as rung X's judge said of the other entries (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/JUDGE.md:13-19`).
38	
39	**The rung's own sentence.** The declared type "extends the entry's type exactly where the constraints hold: an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type, and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:371-374`). So `D[\Fn\]` is a well-formed instance, which is not a `Shows`. Each part of the header states something about every instance:
40	
41	- **The static parameters.** `F extends W[\E\]` bounds `F` at every `E`, and `W[\Fn\]` is ill formed.
42	- **The `excludes` clause.** "neither can extend the other, and no trait can extend them both" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:223-227`), for `D[\E\]` and `W[\E\]` at every `E`.
43	- **The `comprises` clause.** "every type listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause extends \VAR{T}, and every value of type \VAR{T} is a value of one of the listed types" (`traits.tex:235-237`). For `D[\Fn\]` the listed `V[\Fn\]` is not a type.
44	- **An object's contract.** It "is evaluated when the object is created" (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:189-190`), and the constructor `V[\Fn\](x)` is a call at an instance where the condition fails.
45	
46	Checking any of these parts as if the condition held assumes it at instances where, by `:371-374`, it does not hold. This is the argument by which rung X's judge upheld `bd18b6a47` for the other entries (`JUDGE.md:21-26`).
47	
48	**The counter-reading.** `trait-parameters.tex:375` opens "Within the declaration the constraints hold:". The header is syntactically within the declaration. The upheld `bd18b6a47` already reads the sentence more narrowly than the syntax: the other `extends` entries are within the declaration too, and they are checked without the conditions (`:377-378`). The sentence's own colon names what it covers, "the entry itself and the declaration's members". The repair rewrites the sentence to name what holds under the condition and what does not, so the counter-reading has no text left to rest on.
49	
50	**What keeps the conditions.** `Decls` checks the members, the fields and the methods, with the conditions holding (`Decls.scala:88-89`, `:111-120`; `:135-136`, `:165-174`), and that is P-151's rule. An object's non-transient value parameters are its fields: "Each field is either a non-transient value parameter of a constructor declaration, or it is explicitly defined by a field declaration within the body" (`objects.tex:271-272`). So the value parameters stay with the members, as the review's repair has them. `self` is the declaration's self type, which the members are checked against, so it stays with them too. A member checked under the condition stays callable where the condition fails (row 773, in the Effect at `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:221-224`), and the value parameters share that hole. Section 6 lists this line for the curator.
51	
52	**The library.** No library declaration has a header that needs a condition, by reading. The only conditional entries are `List`'s and `PureList`'s (`Library/List.fsi:67-68`, `Library/List.fss:106-107`, `Library/PureList.fss:41-42`). The grep `where *{ *[A-Za-z]* extends` over `Library` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` finds no other in an `extends` clause. The `List` declarations take one unbounded parameter, have no `where` clause of their own, and their `excludes { Number, HasRank, String }` names no static parameter (`List.fsi:69`, `List.fss:108`, `PureList.fss:43`). So the count stays 30 and the distance 34 after the repair. That is by reading; the repair's count runs and the gate measure it. In the corpora, the conditional entries are those of X's four compiled tests and one walk test: `grep -ln "extends *{[^}]*where *{"` over `compiler_tests`, `library_tests`, `other_compiler_tests` and `tests`. None has a static-parameter bound, an own `where` clause, a contract, or an `excludes` or `comprises` clause.

# Climb batch 17: the repair after the merged-diff review

Written 2026-10-17 on `main` above `41567bcc1`, the judge's ruling (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-17/JUDGE-review.md`). The repair carries out the ruling's eleven steps in order, in `/home/user/fortress`, whose build is the merged tree's: `ant compileAll` built nothing and printed "Caches /home/user/fortress/default_repository/caches kept" ("BUILD SUCCESSFUL", "Total time: 2 seconds"), and no path under `ProjectFortress/src` or `Library/` differs from `21dce2148`. Nothing was built but the specification. The machine: nproc 4, Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, 2100 MHz, openjdk 25.0.4.1; each harness run's first line gives the load (0.00 to 0.07).

1. **Where "row 771" goes in PLAN.md.** The review.1 sentence of A.skeptic.1's entry ends "that clause would need the opening to read the constraint first", followed by its citations in parentheses. The row number opens that parenthesis, "(row 771; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-17/RECORD.md`, ...)", rather than standing in a second one beside it. Not taken: "(row 771) (...)", two parentheses in a row.
2. **Where the judge's three items go.** All three under "Off the path, parked", in "Climb batch 17, listed for his review": none asks an answer before work on the path goes on. judge-review.1 joins A.skeptic.1's entry, since it is the fork of the point review.1 raised there, reading the constraint at the opening, and the ruling places it "with A.skeptic.1's answer for `Array`"; the entry's opening names the three ids. judge-review.2 (the comment of `OverloadedFunction.java`) and judge-review.3 (F-252's limit, for the coordinator) are entries of their own, as climb batch 16's judge-review.1 was. Not taken: a separate entry for judge-review.1, which would put one point in two places.
3. **The walk runs.** The ruling's step 2 names one walk run of the program; row 771's notes, from the same ruling, say walk prints 7 "for both". Both forms were run, each from its own scratch folder, since a component's file must carry its name.

\subsection{Conditional extension}
\seclabel{revival-conditional}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
\item[Change] A paragraph and an example are added, with a box: where the
\KWD{where} clause of an entry of an \KWD{extends} clause introduces no
\KWD{where}-clause variable and all its constraints are trait constraints,
the declared trait or object extends the entry's type exactly where the
constraints hold, and within the declaration the constraints hold while the
entry itself and the declaration's members are checked, and not while the
other entries of its \KWD{extends} clause are; the example is
\library's list, totally ordered exactly where its elements are.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
decided on 16~October 2026 to build the forms of \KWD{where} clause the team
wrote down, among them that a trait that extends another under a
\KWD{where} condition is that type only where the condition holds and that
its members are checked under the condition, as Haskell checks an
instance's context, Rust a conditional implementation and Swift a
conditional conformance.
The grammar gives each entry of an \KWD{extends} clause its own optional
\KWD{where} clause, and the text orders lists ``whose elements support these
same comparison operators''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex},
lines 284--285), which no
unconditional declaration of the list type can state:
\library\ declared their list type as lexicographically ordered at every
element type, so the compiled type checker refused the comparison of two
elements of an unbounded type in the order's own body.
The team's internal notes foresaw conditional subtyping and its cost,
that ``we may also not be able to tell whether a trait has a particular
method'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex},
lines 538--543, in its subsection ``No Wrapped Fields Whose Types Are Naked
Type Variables'').
A clause that introduces a \KWD{where}-clause variable, or whose
constraints are not all trait constraints, keeps the reading it had: the
entry is extended at every instance.
\library's list keeps an element-wise \EXP{=} of its own outside the
condition, so that a list whose elements are not ordered, a list of pairs
among them, is still compared element by element.
The alternative not taken is to read the clause as limiting nothing, the
extension holding at every instance, under which the clause has no effect
and the list's order needs another construct.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/REPORT.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker reads such a clause as this
section says: a value of an instance whose static arguments satisfy the
constraints is of the entry's type, one whose static arguments do not is
refused where that type is expected, and the entry and the declaration's
members are checked with the constraints holding, its other entries without
them.
\library's \TYP{LexicographicOrder} bounds its element type by
\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}, and its list extends it under the constraint
that its element type does, so the compiled type checker orders a list
exactly where its elements are totally ordered.
It gives no order to a list of partially ordered elements, of \TYP{RR64},
\TYP{QQ} or ranges among them, where \secref{partial-total-orders} says
that a lexicographic order ``may be partial or total depending on whether the
ordering of the elements is partial or total''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex},
lines 520--522), and where the operators chapter's subsection

lexicographic order of lists is declared.

constraints holding be called where they fail: it accepts a call of such

(row~773 of the revival's gap ledger).
Its other readers of an \KWD{extends} clause, the members a type inherits

lines 483--512, its subsection ``Conditional Subtyping''), is read as
extended at every instance on both paths.

An entry of an \KWD{extends} clause may carry a \KWD{where} clause of its
own (\secref{trait-decls}).

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

set -u

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)

usage: ledger.py [-h] COMMAND ...

The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

positional arguments:
  COMMAND

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`). Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the
record file and its history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or

Initialization of singleton objects is nondeterministic
as described in \chapref{execution}.
The type of an object constructor function is an arrow type
consisting of the object's value parameter type followed by
the token \EXP{\rightarrow}, followed by the object trait type.

---
Fields are variables local to an object.
They must not be referred to outside their enclosing object declarations.
Each field is either a non-transient value parameter of a constructor
declaration, or it is explicitly defined by a field declaration within the body of a constructor
declaration, a singleton declaration, or an object expression
---
\note{Victor: this belongs in the type chapter.}

A trait with an \KWD{excludes} clause excludes
every trait listed in its \KWD{excludes} clause.
If a trait \VAR{T} excludes a trait \VAR{U},
the two traits are mutually exclusive:
neither can extend the other, and no trait can extend them both.
As discussed in \secref{type-relations},
the exclusion relation is symmetric.
Thus, if \VAR{T} excludes \VAR{U}
then \VAR{U} excludes \VAR{T}
whether or not \VAR{T} is listed in an \KWD{excludes} clause
in the declaration of \VAR{U}.

If a trait declaration of \VAR{T} includes a \KWD{comprises} clause
then every type listed in its \KWD{comprises} clause extends \VAR{T},
and every value of type \VAR{T} is a value of one of the listed types.

input.summary: Repair of climb batch 18's merged tree, as the review's judge ruled, with one deviation, recorded in explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-18/REPAIR-review.md. TypeWellFormedChecker's trait and object cases (TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:192-212, :218-236) now check the header with the declaration's own where clause only: the static parameters, own where clause, throws clause, contract, excludes and comprises. The extends entries, the value parameters and the members keep the conditions. A declaration with no conditional entry keeps the base's single analyzer. Four typecheck expected failures pin this: XXXCondExtendExcludesChecker, XXXCondExtendComprisesChecker, XXXCondExtendParamBoundChecker and XXXCondExtendExcludesWhereChecker. All four were red on main before the edit and are 'Saw expected failure' after it, in one JVM with rung X's four tests and rung K's eight: OK (17 tests). ant testQuick: BUILD SUCCESSFUL, compiler track 1270, 4 more than the gate's 1266. Count stage: base 67.8 s, change 68.9 s; the tables are equal and so are the run.txt files. The profile shows no gain (5,059 samples; the edit's extend has 1 sample), so there is no pass and no audit. The deviation: the ruling's fifth test (the object contract) is accepted by the base too. TypeDisambiguator.java:112-113 and :137-138, the team's own lines, drop a trait's and an object's throws clause and contract before any checker sees them. So Decls.scala:139-142 never checks a contract, and no edit the ruling allows can turn that test green. Decls is therefore unchanged, the test is not gated (its text is kept in REPAIR-review.md), and the defect is ledger row 781. The specification (trait-parameters.tex, changes.tex), F-255, RECORD.md:250 and PLAN.md:494 are written as ruled, with the deviation; the Effect adds one sentence naming row 781. The spec build was BUILD SUCCESSFUL twice; its 42 grep lines are the same macro trace batch 17 read. judge-review.1 is a new PLAN entry under 'Off the path, parked'. One local commit 5b11849c6, not pushed; the gate reruns because ProjectFortress/src changed.
decisions: Decls.scala not edited and the contract test (XXXCondExtendContractChecker) not gated. The base's typecheck of it exits 0. TypeDisambiguator.java:112-113 and :137-138 (the team's a874948ac :100-101, :125-126) pass Option.<Contract>none() and Option.<List<Type>>none() for traits and objects, so no contract reaches Decls.scala:139-142. Proof: an object with requires { 1 + "a" } typechecks with exit 0 on the base; the disambiguated tree of an object with requires has no contract; a function's contract is checked ('No such method E.shown.'). Alternatives not taken: a gated red test; an edit of Decls that no program can observe (tests-writing.md, 'The order'); an edit of TypeDisambiguator.java, which the ruling forbids (JUDGE-review.md:76). The ruling's own step-3 fallback (do not edit Decls where it does not reach the contract with the conditions) applies a fortiori.

Added one sentence to the Appendix I Effect naming row 781, because the ruling's 'the rest of the declaration without them' would claim the compiled checker checks a trait's or object's throws clause and contract, which it never sees. The trait-parameters.tex sentence, about the language, stays as ruled.

The (e) key, '9:16-23: No such method E.shown.', comes from the base's refusal of the same contract on a function at the same columns, not from a run of the object; it is kept only in REPAIR-review.md.
